title: Twenty-one calls, five edges
spec: M03 · source → tree → query → graded edges, and the ones the parser refuses to guess
intro: Parse one real orderflow file, run an extraction query over the tree, grade every capture, and finish on the honest part: the call edges a static parser can never resolve, and why refusing to emit them is the feature.

provenance.source: a replayed extraction session over labs/sample-project/shared/auth.py. The S-expression in step 2 is trimmed for reading; the grep hits, definition lines, call-site counts and edge grades in steps 1, 3, 4 and 6 are reproducible with labs/shared_tools/kg_extract.py and are cited per step.

foot: Do it for real in labs/M03-tree-sitter-extraction/README.md — including the fault-tolerance step, which is the one that changes how you think about "the code doesn't compile"

steps.title: One symbol, three different things
narrative: Start with what the alternatives see. Search orderflow for decode_jwt and five lines come back across three files.

One is a definition. One is a call. Three are prose — a runbook sentence, an ASCII diagram, a README bullet. Grep found the string decode_jwt and has no vocabulary for the difference; an embedding search (M02) finds text that talks like decode_jwt, which is worse.

Only a parse tree distinguishes them, because defining, calling and mentioning are three different node types in the grammar. That is the entire reason extractors start with a parser instead of a regex.

steps.title: Parse it — the tree, not the text
narrative: Load the Python grammar, hand tree-sitter the file as bytes (its offsets are byte offsets — the moment a file has a non-ASCII character, str will quietly misalign your names), and take the tree.

What comes back is the same 45 lines reorganised as labeled structure: a module root, a class_definition, two function_definition children, and inside them if_statement, raise_statement, return_statement and call nodes. "Abstract" means it dropped the whitespace and most punctuation and kept the grammar.

Two properties matter more than the tree itself. It parses incrementally — edit one function and only that subtree rebuilds, which is what makes watch mode affordable. And it is fault-tolerant: delete a closing parenthesis and you get an ERROR node island, not a failed file, so a half-written branch costs you one node instead of a whole file's worth of nodes and edges.

steps.title: The query — patterns, not regexes
narrative: A tree is not yet a graph. The second half of every extractor is a set of extraction queries: S-expression patterns matched against the tree, with @captures naming the parts you want out.

Three patterns cover the whole of this file. One captures every function's name. The other two capture call targets — and the split between them is the gotcha that silently costs people every method call in a repo: a call node's function field holds a bare identifier for decode_jwt(…) but an attribute for hmac.new(…). Match only the first and every obj.method() in your codebase disappears.

Run them over auth.py: 2 definition captures and 21 call-site captures, 17 of them distinct names. "Language-specific" is doing real work in the phrase extraction query — a Python function_definition is a Go function_declaration, and Ruby lets you drop the parentheses entirely. The grammar gives you the tree; the queries decide what in it becomes knowledge.

steps.title: Grade every capture — the ladder's bottom rung
narrative: The tree tells you with certainty that something named decode_jwt is called on line 45. It does not tell you which decode_jwt. Binding a name at a use site to the declaration it refers to is name resolution, and it is where structural extraction stops being trivially exact.

The bottom rung of the ladder is a table lookup. Target defined in this module and unambiguous → EXTRACTED, a parse-tree fact. Exactly one definition of that name elsewhere in the repo → INFERRED, a heuristic that is usually right. Two or more candidates → AMBIGUOUS, all of them emitted and none confirmed.

Twenty-one captures collapse to five edges. Sixteen — hmac.new, json.loads, len, time.time and the rest — resolve to nothing in this project and are skipped, not guessed. That skip is the discipline: an extractor that invented edges for stdlib names would produce a bigger graph and a worse one.
steps.claudeSays: Each edge is written with its grade attached, so a consumer downstream can set a confidence floor instead of trusting everything equally.

steps.title: What the parser refuses to guess
narrative: Now the limit, because a walkthrough that stopped at the happy path would be teaching you to over-trust the graph.

orderflow's worker.py registers subscribe("payment.settled", send_receipt), and billing later calls publish("payment.settled", …). The parser sees both calls perfectly and sees nothing of the relationship between them: the actual invocation of send_receipt happens at runtime, through a dict of handlers. Check the graph and send_receipt has zero callers. It is called on every settled payment.

Same story with POOL.execute(…). The tree hands you the attribute name execute and says nothing about what POOL is — in Python, types are suggestions. On orderflow exactly one execute is defined, so the heuristic resolves it INFERRED and happens to be right. Define a second execute anywhere in the repo and the same call site must drop to AMBIGUOUS — nothing about the call changed, only the number of candidates.

And getattr(module, name)() is worse than ambiguous: the callee's name does not exist in the tree at all. No edge is the correct output. The middle rung of the ladder — okf-rs generate --lsp, asking pyright or rust-analyzer via textDocument/definition — buys back the name-collision cases at the cost of startup time and project configuration. It buys back none of the dynamic dispatch.
steps.youDo: Run the extractor over orderflow and look up send_receipt's callers. Then read services/notifications/worker.py and satisfy yourself the graph is wrong-by-omission — and that this is the honest answer, not a bug.

view.text: A tool that guessed at these would produce more edges, more wrong edges, and no way to tell them apart — the graph-world version of M02's confidently-plausible retrieval. The value of the structural layer is not that it knows everything; it is that it labels what it knows. Ask any code-context tool which of its answers are facts and which are guesses. Most of them cannot say.

steps.title: The honest tally
narrative: Scale the same two passes to the whole repo and the numbers come out where you can check them: 36 nodes, 22 edges, 9 EXTRACTED, 13 INFERRED, 0 AMBIGUOUS — plus two runtime dispatches that produce no edge at all, which is the row nobody puts in a benchmark table.

No LLM was involved in any of it. No API key exists in these files, the structural pass costs $0 in tokens, and running it twice produces identical output — which is what makes a graph diff in a pull request mean something.

The number to carry out of this module is not 22. It is the split. Every one of the thirteen guesses happens to be correct on a repo this clean, and "happens to be" is only sayable out loud because the extractor graded itself. That grading is the front half of Graphify, and M04 hands you the production version of it.
